data: Roscosmos / Soviet Academy of Sciences (lead, IKI) — international payload from ESA / CNES / Hungary / Austria / Bulgaria / Czechoslovakia / Poland / East Germany

Identical twin of Vega 1: about 4900 kg in total, including the ~1500 kg descent module (Venus lander + helium aerostat). Launched 6 days after Vega 1 for redundancy + a paired Halley armada solution.

© Roscosmos / IKI / international consortium. Vega 2 launched from Baikonur 1984-12-21, 6 days behind Vega 1. Its descent module landed 1985-06-15 at 7.5°S 177.7°E on Venus, returning soil-composition X-ray spectra (anorthosite-norite-troctolite composition — first chemical analysis of Venusian highland material) before high-temperature failure. The Vega 2 balloon performed identically to Vega 1's at ~54 km, with both balloons drifting at ~240 km/h around the planet in opposite hemispheres for ~46 hours. The flyby bus continued to comet 1P/Halley for closest approach (8030 km) on 1986-03-09 — three days after Vega 1's encounter. Together the Vega buses returned the first close-up images of any cometary nucleus, with Vega 2's data refining Vega 1's position fix and feeding directly into the targeting solution for Giotto's much closer 596 km Halley flyby five days later.

Baikonur Cosmodrome, 1984-12-21 — 6 days after Vega 1. Twin mission, identical hardware, slightly different Venus arrival geometry so the two landers + balloons sampled different regions of the atmosphere + surface.

1985-06-15. Lander touched down on Aphrodite Terra; balloon drifted about 11,100 km at 54 km altitude before its batteries failed. Vega 2 surface samples returned the first X-ray fluorescence chemistry from the highlands — anorthositic, distinct from Vega 1's lowland sampling.

Closest approach 8,030 km from Halley's nucleus on 1986-03-09, three days after Vega 1. Together the two Vegas + Sakigake/Suisei + Giotto delivered the first multi-spacecraft cometary observation campaign in history — pathway-data sharing across NASA, ESA, Roscosmos (then Soviet Intercosmos), and JAXA's predecessors was unprecedented for the period.
First chemical analysis of Venusian highland-type soil (Aphrodite Terra, 1985); paired Halley encounter with Vega 1 fed Giotto's targeting solution

Twin of Vega 1, launched 6 days later (1984-12-21) for redundancy + a paired Halley armada solution. Vega 2's descent module landed 1985-06-15 in Rusalka Planitia, on the northern flank of Aphrodite Terra, and used XRF spectrometry to find anorthosite-norite-troctolite material — the first chemical analysis of highland-type Venusian crust (the composition resembles lunar highlands, though the landing site itself is a plain). Its balloon performed identically to Vega 1's, drifting in the opposite hemisphere at ~240 km/h. The bus flew past comet 1P/Halley at 8030 km on 1986-03-09. Together the two Vega buses returned the first close-up cometary-nucleus images and refined the position fix that allowed Giotto to attempt a 596 km flyby five days later.
